A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, payoff matrices, algorithm, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial proof reorganization.

before.justification: v3 presents theoretical bounds, proofs, and analytically constructed examples. Neither the main text nor appendices report original empirical results.

after.justification: v4 remains theoretical, including its new converse theorem and appendix proof. It reports no experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a proof-specific learner that selects principal-worst approximate best responses and switches to an existing no-swap-regret algorithm upon a principal deviation. The original reduction, Algorithm 1, and mean-based exploitation strategy are retained.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation tasks. Bayesian persuasion, Stackelberg games, and contract design remain theoretical applications in both.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing methods experimentally. References to existing learning algorithms and prior theoretical bounds do not constitute added baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: No experimental protocols, metrics, splits, sample sizes, or training budgets are introduced or revised. Changes to the formal game description concern theoretical modeling.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations or empirical robustness analyses. The mean-based exploitation example and Example 4.1 are retained; the added converse is theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated trials, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Their regret guarantees are mathematical bounds, not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The illustrative payoff matrices, mean-based payoff of approximately 1/2 minus O(sqrt(gamma)), Example 4.1, and application corollaries retain their numerical content. No empirical results are added; the new formal tightness result is assessed under T1.

T1.justification: v4 adds Theorem 3.3 and Appendix B.2, claiming a converse against every adaptive principal strategy through a suitable no-regret or no-swap-regret learner. Combined with the retained Example 4.1, this extends tightness from approximate best response to the repeated learning problem. v4 also explicitly requires |S| >= |A| and adds a revelation-principle justification. Most Section 4 proof changes are relocations.

C1.justification: v4 adds Result 3 as a central contribution and strengthens the headline square-root regret dependence from an achievable guarantee to claimed worst-case tightness, including adaptive principal strategies. The other principal guarantees and mean-based exploitation claim remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds an explanation of the asymmetric bounds through randomized approximate responses, explicitly sets computational complexity outside its scope, and discusses unknown or nonstationary environments and joint learning. It clarifies that private information held by the principal is compatible with the existing framework.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the accompanying contextual-bandit construction are retained despite Appendix A's expanded heading. No implementation settings, hardware information, or code/data access provisions are added.

R1.justification: v4 adds Roughgarden (2016) and expands distinctions from Jain and Perchet and from computational approximate-response research. The core literature remains unchanged; Jain and Perchet's 2023-to-2024 update refers to the same work.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around three questions and four results, and the discussion is rewritten. Separate persuasion and cheap-talk descriptions are consolidated, while Section 4's detailed proof development is reorganized into Appendix C. These changes substantially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v4 consolidates the boxed persuasion/cheap-talk presentations, changes equation display placement, and restyles references with colored links and backreferences. The payoff matrices and Algorithm 1 remain, with no new empirical figures or tables.

improvement.justification: v4 improves exposition and adds a potentially important tightness converse. However, Appendix B.2 conditions its learner's behavior on detecting the principal's current strategy, whereas Section 2.2 makes that strategy unobserved and has the learner choose first. The PDFs do not reconcile these information requirements. This leaves the new central claim's justification unresolved, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the presentation improvements.
